transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. To start, can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, I... I guess I'm here because things at work have gotten to a point where I just can't... I can't take the weight of it anymore. I drive the industrial tractors and forklifts down at the main distribution warehouse, and I have for a long time. I'm 62 now, so I'm one of the old hands down on the floor, you know? I know every bay, every aisle better than anyone. But they have this routing system now. And they tell everybody it's just software, just a program to manage the inventory flow and tell us where to drive. 

But it's not. It isn't just a computer to me anymore, I know exactly what it's doing. 

Every time I pick up a load, I have to use the scanner, and I started noticing a few months ago how it's... it's marking my moves. Not just logging the freight, but *marking* me, tracking my physical location to trap me. It's sending these messages through the scanners, right into the display screen—little codes, specific delays, and routing errors that are specifically designed to push me out. It knows I'm older. It knows I'm an old hand and it wants me gone. I sit up in the cab of my truck for ten, twelve hours a shift, and I just watch it happen, scan after scan. The network is literally communicating with me, threatening me, telling me my time is up by boxing me into these dead-end routes so I'll fail. Nobody else seems to see the messages, or maybe they're just pretending they don't, but I know the machine is trying to force me out the door. It's exhausting, just... constantly being watched and targeted by the walls around you.
Can you tell me exactly when you first started noticing these messages from the scanner system, and has this feeling been continuous since then, or did it come and go?

Well, doctor, if I really think back on it... really trace it back to the beginning, it's been going on for a long time now. A very long time. I'd say it's been about a year and eight months. Yes, a year and eight months since I first realized what was happening. And I remember it so clearly, too, because it was right around the time they did that big software update on the warehouse floor. They brought in all these contractors with their laptops, walking around, pointing at the bays, talking in low voices. And right after that, that's when the voices started. At first, it was just... whispers, you know? Just these low, murmuring sounds coming through the static of the scanner when I'd pick up a pallet of auto parts in Sector 4. I thought it was just interference, maybe a bad radio frequency from the new routers they installed up in the rafters. But then the whispers turned into words, and the words turned into... well, into threats. And the screen, the display on my dash, it started blinking in these patterns. 

And you ask if it comes and goes? No. No, it never really goes away. Not entirely. It's like a heavy blanket that just sits on me, day in and day out. For a year and eight months, I've had to climb into that cab, turn the key, and just brace myself for what the system is going to say to me that day. Sometimes it's louder, sometimes it's more subtle—like it's just waiting, watching me make a mistake. But the fixed belief, the absolute certainty that the system is targeting me, that it wants me gone... that hasn't wavered for a single second. It's always there, doctor. Always. It's exhausting, just... carrying that knowledge around, knowing that the very machine you rely on to do your job is actively conspiring against you. It's been a year and eight months of pure, unadulterated torment, and I just... I don't know how much longer I can keep fighting it.

During this past year and eight months, have you had any distinct periods where you felt persistently very low, hopeless, or lost interest in almost everything, or on the flip side, unusually elated or full of energy, lasting for weeks at a time?

Well, doctor, the low feeling... the hopelessness... that's actually been there even longer than the scanner messages. If I really sit and calculate it, the depression, that heavy, suffocating feeling where I just can't find the point in anything anymore, that's been hanging over me for about two years and one month now. Yes, two years and a month. 

I know the exact timeline because it all started not long after they messed with our shifts. They did this massive schedule change, moving us from the standard rotation to these grueling, unpredictable swing shifts. They said it was for "efficiency," to keep the warehouse running 24/7 without paying overtime, but it just destroyed my routine. I'd be working days one week, nights the next, and my body just... it couldn't take it. I started feeling so worn down, so incredibly drained. I'd come home to my empty apartment, sit in the recliner, and just stare at the wall. I didn't want to eat, didn't want to watch the game, didn't want to talk to anyone. I just felt this deep, dark pit open up inside me, and I fell right in. 

And it hasn't let up. For over two years now, every single day feels like I'm trying to walk through wet cement. The joy is just... gone. Completely drained out of me. I used to like tinkering with old radios on the weekends, you know? Taking them apart, fixing the vacuum tubes, getting them to catch a signal again. I haven't touched my workbench in two years. I just look at the tools and think, "What's the point?" It's just this constant, crushing weight. 

But as for the other thing you mentioned... feeling unusually elated or full of energy? No. Never. I haven't felt a drop of real energy in so long I don't even remember what it feels like. There are no highs, doctor. None at all. Just this long, endless, exhausting low that started with that schedule change two years and a month ago and just... never left. It just sits there, right alongside the system trying to force me out. It's like I'm fighting a war on two fronts, and I'm losing both of them.

Have there been any times in the past year and eight months when your mood felt a bit better or less heavy, and if so, did the messages from the scanner and the voices continue during those times as well?

Well, doctor, if I really search my memory... there was this one stretch. Just one, really, where that heavy, wet cement feeling I told you about kind of... I don't know, it eased up a little bit. It was maybe for a few weeks. I actually remember I went down to the grocery store and bought real food—some sliced deli ham, a loaf of decent rye bread, things like that—instead of just staring at the empty pantry. I was eating a little more, actually having an appetite for the first time in God knows how long. And I was talking a little more, too. I even stood out by the mailboxes and had a whole conversation with the fella next door about the parking situation at our complex, which I normally would have just put my head down and walked right past. 

But... if you're asking if the system gave me a break just because I was feeling a little more like a human being? No. Absolutely not. 

Even during that stretch, for those several weeks where my mood had eased some, the torment down at the warehouse didn't stop for a single second. I still heard dispatch calling my number through the static in the cab. Clear as a bell. I'd be driving the forklift, maybe feeling just a fraction lighter that morning, and then I'd hear it—my specific employee ID, coming through the scanner, telling me I was out of time. I still believed, with every bone in my body, that the routing system was tracking me. I knew it was watching my physical location, logging every turn I made down the aisles, just waiting for me to slip up so they could fire me. So the dark cloud over my head might have parted just a crack for a few weeks, but the machine... the machine never stopped tracking me. It just kept right on going, doctor, right on plotting against me, no matter how I felt.

I... I'm sorry, doctor, you're going to have to repeat that. I didn't quite catch what you just asked. I know you were just speaking, but my mind, it just... it pulls me right back to the warehouse floor. It's like a magnet, you know? I sit here in this nice, quiet office of yours, but in my head, I'm still smelling the cardboard dust and the hydraulic fluid from the lift. I'm just sitting there bracing myself for that scanner to blink, waiting for the system to make its move against me. 

It’s a terrible thing, really, not being able to just stay present, not being able to just sit in a chair and have a normal conversation without the dispatch radio creeping into my thoughts. I try to focus on your words, I really do, but the static... it's like it's permanently etched into my eardrums now, playing over and over. So, if you wouldn't mind, could you ask me that again? What did you mean just now? I'll try to keep my mind right here in the room this time, I promise.

Doctor, I... I just realized you didn't ask a question. You didn't say anything at all, did you? You were just sitting there, waiting for me, and I... I just filled in the blank. I thought you had spoken. I'm sorry. I really am. It's just that the silence in here, it gets so loud sometimes. When it's quiet, that's when the warehouse really rushes in to fill the space. 

It's like... well, it's like when you're driving home after a twelve-hour shift, and you turn off the engine of your car, but you can still feel the vibration of the forklift in your bones, you know? You can still hear the hum of the engine and the beeping of the reverse alarm echoing in your head. That's what it's like for me, all the time now. Even sitting here with you. The silence is just a canvas for the system to paint its threats on. 

I was so sure you had asked me something about the scanner, or the dispatch voices, or maybe even about the schedule change again. My mind just raced ahead, anticipating the next interrogation, the next piece of evidence they're going to use against me. Because that's what they do, doctor. They gather data. Every second of every day, they're gathering data. And I just assumed you were doing the same thing. 

But you didn't say anything, did you? You just let me ramble on, exposing myself, showing you exactly how fractured my attention is, how easily I get pulled away by the static. I apologize for that. I really do try to stay focused, to be a good patient, to answer your questions accurately. But it's just so hard when there's this constant, overwhelming pressure bearing down on me, this feeling that I have to defend myself against an invisible enemy that's always watching, always listening, always waiting for me to make a mistake. 

So, please, if you do have a question, go ahead and ask. I'm listening now. I really am. I'll try my best to keep the warehouse out of it, to just focus on you and what you're saying. I just... I need you to understand how hard it is, how much effort it takes just to stay in this room, in this chair, when my mind is a million miles away, trapped in that concrete box with the hydraulic fluid and the cardboard dust and the scanner that never stops blinking.

You see, alcohol... it slows your reaction time, doesn't it? It dulls your senses. And I can't afford to be dull. Not for a single second. But it's more than just the safety protocols, really. If I have even one beer at home, my mind gets a little foggy, and that's exactly when the system would strike. I have to stay vigilant. I don't need some pill or some weed making the dispatch radio harder to decipher. I need to be able to hear exactly what they're plotting against me. If I'm high, I'm vulnerable. I can't be vulnerable.

As for supplements or new medications... no. I don't trust any of that stuff. You go to the pharmacy and buy a plastic bottle of vitamins, but how do you really know what's in those capsules? You don't. The manufacturers, the shipping logs, the distribution centers... it's all part of a massive supply chain, and I know exactly how supply chains work. I've worked in them my whole life. Things can be inserted. Pallets get swapped. They could easily slip something into a supplement bottle to make me more compliant, or to make the ringing in my ears louder, just to break me down faster. I can't take that risk. 

I just stick to tap water and black coffee. Lots of black coffee, just to keep my eyes open and my head as clear as it can be, considering... well, considering everything else that's going on in there. So, no. No drugs, no alcohol, no vitamins. There's nothing in my system but caffeine and fear, doctor. That's all I'm running on these days.

Was it the part about the supply chains? I shouldn't have mentioned the distribution centers, should I? That's what triggered this, isn't it? You're probably thinking I'm reading too much into it, but I know how these things work. I've spent thirty-five years on the floor, moving freight, scanning barcodes, watching how everything connects. 

When you just sit there and don't respond, it feels exactly like when they pull you into the glass office on the mezzanine level back at the warehouse. The floor manager, he does this exact same thing. He pulls up your pick-rate on his monitor, and he just lets the silence hang there in the air. He wants you to sweat. He wants you to start talking, to nervously explain why you were three seconds late scanning a bin on aisle seven, even though there was a pallet of dog food spilled everywhere and maintenance hadn't cleared it yet. They don't care about the spill, doctor. They only care about the data. And right now, sitting here in this quiet, I feel like you're just collecting data on me. 

I mean, I just told you I'm running on nothing but caffeine and fear, and... nothing? Not even a nod? It makes my mind race. It makes the static come back. If you don't talk, the dispatch radio in my head just turns up the volume to fill the void. I can hear them calling out bay numbers right now. Bay 12, Bay 14... they're staging a load, and I'm supposed to be on the forklift, but I'm here, and you're not saying anything. 

Please, you have to guide me here. I told you how hard it is to stay focused in this room. If you leave empty space, the warehouse just floods right back in. The smell of the damp cardboard, the hydraulic fluid, the heavy hum of the engine vibrating right up through my boots... it's all right here in this office the second you stop talking. Just ask me another question. Anything at all. What else do you need to know? Because this silence... it's practically a weapon at this point.

I was still hearing them call my number, and the routing system was tracking my every move the exact same as before. It didn't care that I was in a better mood. It just kept tracking me.
